title: The Incarnation and Christ's High Priesthood
english: …The death resulting from the attacks of beasts is rendered weak in its aftermath.
For it was not possible to surrender life to death.
For he does not seize upon demons, but rather he takes hold of the seed of Abraham, from which it was necessary for him to be made like his brothers in every respect.

If the Only-begotten Word of God had not become man, and had instead assumed the human countenance unto himself—as those who discern [the mystery] seem to suggest, that it occurred through good-will alone or by a mere inclination of will—how could he have been made like his brothers in all things? Furthermore, how could anyone fully conceive of him as a brother, when he is the one who transcends all, surpassing those incomparable excellencies which I call natural, and surpassing even creation? How could he have shared in blood and flesh unless these things had become his own, just as they are ours? Thus, there is truly one Son and Lord, having been joined in unity of subsistence through the Word's participation in human flesh and blood and having been made like his brothers in every respect.
This was so that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest.

Moses, the divinely inspired lawgiver, came to bring Israel into the knowledge of God through type and shadow, and showed the way of righteousness through the law; yet he was slow of voice and slow of tongue.
Because of this, the God of all was known even to those in Judah alone, from Dan even unto Beersheba, and by the river and the sea.
For these are the boundaries of the land of the Jews.
And his name was great and most widely known.

Seeing this, the prophet David sings a psalm and speaks concerning those from Israel, saying, 'A vine you brought up out of Egypt; you expelled the nations and uprooted her' (Psalm 80:9). He applies this to the borders reaching the Euphrates river, and indeed even to the sea toward the south and to India, limiting the territory of the Jews: 'He stretched out its camps even to the sea, and its branches even to the rivers' (Psalm 80:10). Thus, even though it was contracted to barely encompass the nations, the proclamation of the all-wise Moses is seen; he offers to those called by obedience the honors and the fleeting, imminent rewards of life under the law.
I say that he names the land of promise everywhere.
For the law has justified no one.

No one is justified in the law before God, for it is 'impossible for the blood of goats and of bulls to take away sin' (Hebrews 10:4). But our Lord Jesus Christ has become a merciful and faithful High Priest for the propitiation of the sins of the people, and in Him, having been tested, He was helped by those who are being tested.

For He has called the inhabited world to a holy and heavenly calling, and He has become High Priest; for He was not a minister of the law that condemns, but rather, through forgetfulness and by grace and love, He has justified through faith and has granted us the washing of the ancient sins.

For being both always and by nature merciful, His only-begotten Word has been set as our mediator and the mediator of God through the Incarnation, so that just as He was always kind and merciful, so indeed, having been shown as High Priest again, He dwells among those on the earth, acting as a friend to those who are beloved by Him and not departing from His own…

title: Heavenly Citizenship in Christ
english: Heavenly indeed, and most fittingly, he names the vocation that comes through Christ. For the God of all graciously bestows on those summoned through him not fleeting blessings nor the transient gifts given by the law through Moses to the ancients, but rather the very things that those once called have chosen—namely, eternal life—which he sustains and secures as an irrevocable possession.

We too have been designated heavenly in another way, with Christ taking the lead, and the way and the door having become ours. And truly Paul says, 'Just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the heavenly' (1 Corinthians 15:49), and again, 'The first man is from the earth, earthly; the second is from heaven' (1 Corinthians 15:47). Such as the earthly one is, such are the earthly people; and such as the heavenly one is, such are the heavenly people. Therefore we have become heavenly, for we are being shaped into Christ through the Spirit, who comes from heaven.

And because of this, even as we walk upon the earth, we hold our citizenship in heaven. We have not approached in equal measure the ancient manifestations of God—those accompanied by blazing fire, darkness, gloom, tempest, trumpet blast, and the voice of words—but we have drawn near rather to Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, amidst myriads of angels in festal assembly, the congregation of the firstborn whose names are inscribed in heaven, before the Judge who is God of all, and the spirits of the just made perfect.

title: Faithfulness of Jesus
english: Having been perfected and inaugurated as the mediator of a new covenant, Jesus speaks with a blood superior to Abel's, for while Abel's blood cried out against his murderer and brother-killer, Jesus' precious blood not only pleads for mercy from the Father on behalf of the world but also cleanses us for justification through its sanctifying power. Therefore, we ought to consider Jesus, the apostle and high priest of our confession, who remained faithful to the One who appointed him.

He is indeed a high priest and apostle who proved faithful even unto death and the cross, having offered himself in accordance with the Father's good pleasure, so that we might become his imitators, unafraid to endure death should it come to us through piety and obedience to God. The blessed Peter affirms this, declaring that Christ died for us, leaving us an example to follow in his footsteps, and the Savior himself declares that whoever wishes to follow him must deny themselves, take up their cross, and follow him, as stated in Matthew 16:24.

To call the Son faithful does not diminish his glory, for this attribute is most befitting of God and the Father alone. As it is written, God is faithful, and there is no unrighteousness in him; he is righteous and holy, the Lord. One of Christ's disciples taught that those who suffer according to God's will should commit their souls to the faithful Creator, and Paul affirmed that God is faithful, through whom we were called into fellowship with his Son. In these contexts, 'faithful' signifies nothing less than what is safe, reliable, and worthy of trust in regard to what God says or does.

The Son demonstrated this faithfulness to the Father even in his humanity, enduring the cross and death to fulfill what he knew to be right. He declared that he came down from heaven not to do his own will but the will of the One who sent him, as recorded in John 6:38. And this is the will of the One who sent him: that he should lose nothing of all that has been given him, but raise it up on the last day, as also stated in John 6:39-40. We were given to the Son as Savior and life-giver, and this was the work entrusted to him by the Father.

For the Father accomplishes all that he wills through the Son in a manner worthy of God, because the Son is the Father's power and wisdom. The Son himself testified that his witness is greater than John's, for the works the Father gave him to complete bear witness that the Father sent him. David also sang, 'Command, O God, your power; strengthen, O God, what you have worked in us.' Let us consider, if it seems right, what kind of priesthood the Son possesses—whether it is servile and ministering to another's glory, or whether it rightly belongs to the Son himself.
